title: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin & Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (1868–1921 / 1900–1979 / 1910–1995) — Harvard's 30-Cent-an-Hour Cepheid Yardstick, the Suppressed 1925 Hydrogen-Star Thesis, and the 1.44-Solar-Mass Degeneracy Limit Mocked by Eddington

teenKit.tldr: Three sidelined outsiders working in the shadows of early 20th-century astronomy cracked how far away stars are, what they are made of, and how heavy a dead star can get before it collapses. Their forced-from-the-margins breakthroughs became the skeleton of modern cosmology.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Every time modern telescopes map the expansion of the universe or detect colliding black holes, they are riding on the exact mathematical yardsticks and stellar rules discovered by people the scientific establishment tried to ignore.
keyTakeaways: Henrietta Swan Leavitt mapped 1,777 variable stars while earning 30 cents an hour, discovering a cosmic yardstick that proved the universe is vastly larger than anyone imagined.

Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin combined quantum physics with starlight to prove that stars are made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, despite being pressured by her boss to call her own correct conclusion 'almost certainly not real.'

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated the exact mass limit where a dying white dwarf star collapses, surviving a brutal public humiliation by the establishment leader Arthur Eddington before winning the Nobel Prize decades later.

vocab.meaning: A pulsating star whose regular brightening and dimming allows astronomers to calculate its exact distance from Earth.
The rainbow of colors and dark lines produced when starlight passes through a prism, acting like a chemical barcode for what elements are inside the star.
A quantum mechanical rule that stops subatomic particles from being crushed into the same space, acting as the ultimate shield holding up dead white dwarf stars.
The magic mass ceiling of about 1.44 times our Sun; if a white dwarf star gets heavier than this, it collapses into a neutron star or black hole.

quiz.question: Why wasn't Henrietta Swan Leavitt allowed to use the great refractor telescope at Harvard College Observatory?
options: She didn't know how to operate heavy machinery.
Victorian propriety dictated that a woman's constitution couldn't handle the cold night air.
She was completely blind and relied entirely on glass plates.
She preferred working indoors with magnifying tools.
quiz.explanation: Victorian social rules barred women from night observing under the absurd assumption that the cold air would harm them.

quiz.question: What groundbreaking discovery did Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin make about the composition of stars?
options: Stars are made of the exact same heavy iron-rich rocks found on Earth.
Stars are composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, contrary to the scientific consensus of her time.
Stars contain no gases lighter than carbon and nitrogen.
Stars are solid metallic spheres powered by internal friction.
quiz.explanation: Payne proved that stars are roughly 98 percent hydrogen and helium, shocking an astronomical community that assumed stars shared Earth's heavy-element makeup.

quiz.question: What is the significance of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's 1.44-solar-mass limit?
options: It is the maximum weight a white dwarf star can reach before quantum pressure fails and it collapses.
It is the minimum speed required for a rocket to escape a black hole.
It is the exact amount of hydrogen consumed by the Sun every second.
It is the salary adjustment scientists received for discovering a new galaxy.
quiz.explanation: Chandrasekhar proved that if a white dwarf star exceeds 1.44 times the mass of our Sun, degeneracy pressure fails and the star must collapse further.
